lesson.title: Operant Conditioning: When Consequences Shape Behavior
lesson.summary: Operant conditioning is a form of learning in which the likelihood of a voluntary behavior increases or decreases based on the consequences that follow it, rather than being triggered automatically by a paired stimulus.
lesson.body:
Classical conditioning explains how a neutral stimulus can come to trigger an automatic, reflexive response. It does not explain, though, why an animal presses a lever, why a student studies harder after getting a good grade, or why a child stops touching a hot stove after being burned once. Those are voluntary behaviors, not reflexes, and the process that governs them is operant conditioning: learning in which the consequences that follow a behavior change how likely that behavior is to happen again.

The groundwork for this idea came from Edward Thorndike, who studied cats trying to escape from puzzle boxes and proposed what he called the law of effect: behaviors followed by satisfying outcomes become more likely to be repeated, while behaviors followed by unsatisfying outcomes become less likely. B.F. Skinner built on this foundation and turned it into a rigorous, systematic research program. Skinner developed the operant conditioning chamber, often just called a Skinner box, a controlled enclosure where an animal such as a rat or pigeon could perform a simple, precisely defined behavior, such as pressing a lever or pecking a lit key, and have the consequence of that behavior, such as delivery of a food pellet, controlled and recorded automatically.

The Skinner box mattered as much for its scientific method as for what it revealed. It let researchers hold nearly everything constant except the one variable they wanted to study, and it produced an objective, continuously recorded measure of behavior, the rate of lever presses or key pecks, rather than relying on a human observer's subjective impression. That combination, a clearly defined behavior, a controlled apparatus, and an objective measurement, is what allowed operant conditioning to be studied with the same rigor as any other experimental science, and it is why Skinner's findings held up so well and generalized so broadly.

The central discovery from this research program is that consequences come in a small number of basic types, and getting the terminology exactly right matters, because it is one of the most commonly confused ideas in all of psychology. Consequences can either increase a behavior, called reinforcement, or decrease it, called punishment, and in each case that can happen either by adding something to the situation or by removing something from it. Those four combinations, positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, positive punishment, and negative punishment, are the building blocks covered next.
